citation.title: An Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Design Method for Topology Optimization without Pre-Optimized Training Data
citation.authors: Alex Halle; Lucio Flavio Campanile; Alexander Hasse
citation.version_coded: Version of record; related arXiv preprint 2012.06384

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: After one training phase, the predictor produces designs similar to conventional topology optimization with much lower per-design computational effort.
claim.key_phrase: only a fraction of the computational effort
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Table 5, p. 19: conventional tTO = 1.9 s and PEN prediction tp = 7.3 ms; 1.9 / 0.0073 = 260.3. This excludes training, which the paper treats separately via break-even analysis.
claim.alternatives: Section 3.2 reports 3.25 h training, about 7.6 million randomly generated training points, and a break-even calculation.

baseline.implementation: Sigmund/Andreassen 88-line MATLAB implementation cited as top88
baseline.solver: not stated; authors note sparse solvers could reduce time (Conclusion)
baseline.hardware_classical: Table 1 system: Nvidia Titan RTX 24 GB; AMD Ryzen Threadripper 2950X 16-Core; 128 GB RAM; Windows 10 1909
baseline.hardware_ml: Table 1 system: Nvidia Titan RTX 24 GB; AMD Ryzen Threadripper 2950X 16-Core; 128 GB RAM; Windows 10 1909
baseline.data_generation_cost: About 7.6 million random training points generated during training; separate generation time not reported (Section 3.2)
baseline.quality_metric: compliance, volume fraction and elementwise density difference against top88 results
baseline.quality_gap: For 100 validation inputs, 79.9% of PEN geometry elements differ in density by less than 1% from conventional results (Table 4); volume fraction deviation is nonzero

R1.evidence: Section 3.2/Table 4 reports similarity over 100 matched input cases, but the PEN volume fraction is not exactly constrained and the classical stopping criterion is not stated.

R2.evidence: Conclusion notes the displacement calculation and says faster algorithms such as sparse solvers could remove the stated limitation; no direct stronger-baseline timing is given.

R3.evidence: Section 3.2 and Table 5 report training duration, prediction and classical times, and an explicit break-even calculation that includes training; random-point generation is part of the training process.

R4.evidence: Sections 2.7 and 3.2 evaluate generated designs using compliance and volume criteria, but the paper does not report infeasible/failure rates across outputs.

notes: Full text read from publisher-hosted open-access copy: https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/applsci/applsci-11-09041/article_deploy/applsci-11-09041-v2.pdf. The paper states validation data and predictor model are downloadable; no public runnable source code or licence was located in the article.
